reader_question: Do rents run higher where renters earn more, with each state sized by its renter households?
title: Higher rents went with higher renter incomes across the states in 2025, and Florida’s 3.0 million renter households paid the largest share of income in rent, 35.5 percent.
measure_line: Median gross rent a month against renter households’ median income a year, 2025, 50 states and DC; each circle is a state, its area set by its renter households.
reading_guide: States to the right have renters with higher incomes, and states higher up have higher rents. A larger circle holds more renter households.
notes: This shows the two move together; it does not show one causes the other.

Rent as a percent of income is the Census Bureau’s own measure: the median, across renter households paying cash rent, of each one’s rent over its income. Florida’s 35.5 percent carries a margin of error of 0.5 point at 90 percent confidence, and California’s 32.9 percent, the next highest, 0.3 point.
alt: A bubble chart of 50 states and DC: median gross rent against renter households’ median income in 2025, each circle sized by renter households. The circles climb from lower left to upper right; California’s 6.2 million renter households make the largest circle, at the top right. Florida, in dark ink, sits above the cloud with the largest rent share, 35.5 percent.

table.caption: Rent, renter income and renter households by state, 2025

columns.label: Rent as a percent of income

chart_notes: Florida takes the dark ink; the other states are light gray circles with thin outlines, with California and North Dakota named. The open ring marks the United States. The key gives circles for 0.5, 2 and 6 million renter households.
